messages.subject: Re:  Posterior Predictive Check
parts:
Hi, Daniel. Unfortunately my physics training is rusty (it’s been almost 30 years since I got my physics degree!). What you are doing sounds a bit like what Cook, Rubin, and I discuss in our 2006 paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/Cook_Software_Validation.pdf
But, as we discuss there, to really get the quantiles to do what they’re supposed to, you need to draw parameters from the prior.
But I expect that I’m not really undestanding what’s going on in your case!
Andrew

> On Jul 30, 2015, at 10:20 AM, Daniel Berman <daniel....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Dr. Gelman,
>
> I am working on a project involving Stan and I have a question I wanted to ask you regarding posterior predictive checks. The subject of my project is quantum mechanics and the purpose of my code is to estimate N operators (matrices) in the presence of noise, compared to known noiseless operators. Since I am performing a simulation, I know what the noisy operators should be.
>
> I have a metric, called the trace distance, for comparing the closeness of two operators, which reduces the N estimated operators to N real numbers. So I see how close the estimated operators are to the known noisy operators. These real numbers not explicitly random variables, as they are a function of the estimated operators, and can be calculated in Stan.
>
> I want to see if my estimates are better than assuming noiseless operators. From what I have read, posterior predictive checks seem to be the best approach to do this. Since I am working on self-taught knowledge, I wanted to ensure that my approach to a posterior predictive test makes sense: My idea is to extract the estimates for trace distance produced from the stan() function in R and observe what proportion of trace distances for my estimates are better than the trace distance for the known operators. Does this make sense?
>
> Thanks,
>
> Daniel Berman
